    Content from Geoprocessing in Python

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What are the everyday geoprocessing operations, and what does each one produce?
    • Why must a layer be projected before buffering or measuring?
    • How do I estimate how many people live in a zone that cuts across census tracts?
    • How do I do all of this with GeoPandas?

    Objectives

    • Explain buffer, dissolve, clip, intersect, difference and nearest join, and choose the right one
    • Select features by location and explain how the choice of spatial predicate changes the answer
    • Estimate a population inside a zone with areal weighting, and state the assumption behind it
    • Measure straight-line distances to the nearest facility and recognize their limits
    • Run each operation in GeoPandas on real Lafayette data

    What is geoprocessing?

    Geoprocessing means operations that take one or more spatial layers and produce a new layer: a zone around every store, the parts of tracts inside a city, the distance from each neighborhood to its nearest clinic. A small set of operations covers most everyday GIS work, and every GIS program (QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, GeoPandas, R’s sf) offers the same ones under similar names.

    This episode answers one question with them: how many people in Lafayette and West Lafayette live within 1 mile of a supermarket? The Geoprocessing in QGIS episode answers the same question with the same data by pointing and clicking, so you can follow either one (or both) and compare results.

    The operations

    Operation Question it answers Output GeoPandas
    Buffer What is within d meters of each feature? One polygon per feature layer.buffer(d)
    Dissolve What is the combined area, or the total per group? Merged features layer.dissolve(by=..., aggfunc=...)
    Select by location Which features touch, contain or lie within another layer? A subset (no new shapes) layer[layer.intersects(shape)]
    Clip What part of this layer lies inside a boundary? Cut shapes, own attributes only gpd.clip(layer, boundary)
    Intersect Where do two layers overlap? Cut shapes, attributes of both gpd.overlay(a, b, how="intersection")
    Difference What part of A lies outside B? Cut shapes of A gpd.overlay(a, b, how="difference")
    Nearest join What is the closest feature, and how far is it? Each row plus the nearest match and a distance gpd.sjoin_nearest(a, b, distance_col=...)

    Two habits make the difference between a result you can trust and one you cannot:

    • Clip versus intersect. Both cut shapes. Clip only uses the second layer as a cookie cutter; intersect also copies its attributes onto every piece. Use intersect when you need to know which zone each piece is in.
    • Keep the original area. Once a tract is cut, you can no longer tell what share of it remains. Store its area in a column before any clip or intersect.

    Projection comes first

    A buffer distance and a measured area are in the units of the layer’s coordinate reference system (CRS). Data from the web usually arrives in EPSG:4326, latitude and longitude in degrees. buffer(1609) on such a layer draws a circle 1,609 degrees wide, larger than the planet. A small value such as buffer(0.015) looks plausible but is still wrong: in Indiana a degree of longitude is about 85 km and a degree of latitude about 111 km, so the “circle” is an ellipse. GeoPandas warns you (“Geometry is in a geographic CRS”); take the warning seriously.

    Convert every layer to a projected CRS in meters first. For Indiana, EPSG:26916 (UTM zone 16N) is the usual choice for local work. All layers in an operation must also share the same CRS; GeoPandas refuses to overlay layers with different ones. Foundations notebook 4b and the Data Management module’s Coordinate Reference Systems episode cover the theory.

    Choosing a distance

    A buffer is only as meaningful as its distance. Common thresholds in access research:

    Distance Roughly Typical use
    400 m (a quarter mile) 5-minute walk Bus stops, small parks
    800 m (a half mile) 10-minute walk Parks, transit stations, corner stores
    1.6 km (1 mile) 20-minute walk Supermarkets in urban areas (the USDA’s urban threshold)
    16 km (10 miles) Short drive Supermarkets in rural areas (the USDA’s rural threshold)

    Choose the distance from the literature or from a policy you are evaluating, write it down, and test whether your conclusion changes with a smaller or larger value. That last step is a sensitivity analysis, and it is cheap: change one number and rerun.

    Selecting by location

    Select by location keeps the features of one layer that pass a spatial predicate against another:

    Predicate True when
    intersects The shapes share any point (touching counts)
    within The feature is completely inside the other shape
    contains The other shape is completely inside the feature
    centroid within The feature’s center point is inside the other shape

    The predicate changes the answer, sometimes dramatically. With the 1-mile supermarket zone in Lafayette, 35 tracts intersect it, only 6 lie completely within it, and 24 have their center inside it. None of these is wrong, but a report that says “24 tracts are near a supermarket” must say which test produced that number.

    From areas to people: areal weighting

    Tracts do not line up with buffers or city limits, so a tract is often split. If 40% of a tract’s area falls in the 1-mile zone, how many of its residents live there? Areal weighting assumes they are spread evenly, so it assigns 40% of the population:

    estimated people in a piece = tract population × (piece area ÷ tract area)

    It is simple and transparent, and it is wrong in a predictable way: people live in houses, not in fields, parks, rivers or parking lots. Areal weighting overestimates people in empty parts of a tract and underestimates them in dense parts. It works best when the pieces are large or the tracts uniformly built up. Better methods use smaller units (block groups, blocks) or ancillary data such as land cover, a technique called dasymetric mapping. The Raster Analysis episode shows how land cover can be summarized by tract, which is the first step.

    Applied to Lafayette, areal weighting estimates about 114,000 residents inside the two cities (the 2020 Census counted about 115,000), and about 68% of them within 1 mile of a supermarket.

    Counts, rates and dissolving

    dissolve(by="column", aggfunc="sum") merges features with the same value and adds up their numbers. Summing is right for counts (people, households, households without a car) and wrong for rates and medians (poverty rate, median income). To get a rate for a merged area, sum the numerator and the denominator separately and divide. For a median there is no exact shortcut; use a population-weighted average as an approximation and say so.

    Distance to the nearest facility

    A buffer gives a yes or no answer. A nearest join keeps the detail: it matches every feature (here, each tract’s center point) to its closest supermarket and records the distance. Two practical points:

    • Ties. If two stores are exactly equally close, sjoin_nearest() returns both, adding a row. Always compare row counts before and after.
    • Distance to a polygon is measured to its nearest edge, not its center, which is usually what you want for parks or service areas.

    Pitfalls

    • Edge effects. The store layer covers only the two cities. A rural tract near the county line may have a supermarket just outside the data, so this episode limits the analysis to the city limits. Always ask what lies just beyond your study area.
    • Straight line is not travel. Rivers, railroads and highways turn a 1-mile straight line into a much longer trip. The Network Analysis episode, and Grocery Access Part 2 in the Case Studies module, measure along roads instead.
    • Centroids are not people. A tract center can fall in a field. Population-weighted centers or smaller units give fairer distances.
    • The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP). Results change when the same data is grouped into different units (tracts versus block groups). Note it as a limitation; the Spatial Autocorrelation episode returns to it.
    • Data currency. OpenStreetMap stores open and close. Check the data against local knowledge.
    Callout

    The same analysis in QGIS

    Every step here has a QGIS tool with nearly the same name (Buffer, Dissolve, Select by Location, Clip, Intersection, Difference, Join Attributes by Nearest). The Geoprocessing in QGIS episode walks through them with the same layers, and the numbers should match.

    The workflow in code

    The three notebooks build the analysis step by step. In outline:

    PYTHON 

    import geopandas as gpd

stores = gpd.read_file(stores_url).to_crs(epsg=26916)           # project first
supermarkets = stores[stores["store_type"] == "Supermarket"]

zone = supermarkets.buffer(1609)                                  # buffer: 1 mile in meters
zone = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=zone).dissolve()                 # dissolve the overlaps

tracts["tract_m2"] = tracts.area                                  # keep the original area
in_city = gpd.clip(tracts, city)                                  # clip to the city
pieces = gpd.overlay(in_city, zone, how="intersection")           # intersect with the zone
pieces["pop_near"] = pieces.area / pieces["tract_m2"] * pieces["total_pop"]   # areal weighting
    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Which operation?

    Name the operation (or operations) for each task.

    1. Show the parts of Tippecanoe County that are within 500 m of the Wabash River.
    2. Count the households in each tract that live within 500 m of the river.
    3. Keep only the bus stops that lie inside the West Lafayette city limits.
    4. Find the closest library to each school, and how far away it is.
    1. Buffer the river by 500 m (projected first), then dissolve if it is made of several segments.
    2. Intersect the tracts with the dissolved buffer, then areal weighting on the households column. Keep each tract’s original area before intersecting.
    3. Select by location with within (or clip, which gives the same points for a point layer).
    4. Nearest join (sjoin_nearest with distance_col).
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Spot the mistake

    A classmate’s notebook claims that 100% of the city’s residents live within 1 mile of a supermarket. Their code starts with stores = gpd.read_file(url) and goes straight to stores.buffer(1609). What went wrong, and how do you fix it?

    The layer is still in EPSG:4326, so the buffer distance was read as 1,609 degrees: each buffer covers the whole planet, and every tract falls inside it. Fix: add .to_crs(epsg=26916) right after reading every layer, then buffer by 1609 meters. Check stores.crs before any measurement.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Is the estimate too high or too low?

    Census Tract 104 contains most of Purdue’s residence halls and also large areas of lawns and playing fields. Half of the tract’s area lies inside a park’s 800 m buffer, and the buffered half is mostly playing fields. Will areal weighting overestimate or underestimate the residents near the park? What would improve the estimate?

    It will overestimate: areal weighting puts half the residents in the buffered half, but few people live on the playing fields. Better estimates use smaller units (census blocks), or land cover to move people onto developed land (dasymetric mapping, previewed in the Raster Analysis episode). At minimum, report the assumption and check the tract on a basemap.

    Key Points
    • Project every layer to a CRS in meters (EPSG:26916 for Indiana) before buffering, measuring or overlaying
    • Buffer draws zones, dissolve merges them, clip and intersect cut shapes, difference keeps what lies outside, and a nearest join finds the closest feature and its distance
    • The spatial predicate (intersects, within, centroid within) changes which features are selected; report it
    • Keep the original area before cutting, so areal weighting can split counts by area share
    • Sum counts, never rates or medians; areal weighting assumes an even spread and straight lines are not travel

    Notebooks

    Notebook What you will do
    1a. Buffers and Selecting by Location Buffer Lafayette supermarkets by 1 mile, see what a buffer in degrees does, dissolve the zones and compare three ways of selecting tracts
    1b. Clip, Intersect and Dissolve Clip tracts to the city, estimate the population within 1 mile with areal weighting, and total households without a car near and far
    1c. Distance and Nearest Features Find the nearest supermarket (and park) to every tract center and map the distances

    Overview

    Questions

    • What are the everyday geoprocessing operations, and what does each one produce?
    • Why must a layer be projected before buffering or measuring?
    • How do I estimate how many people live in a zone that cuts across census tracts?
    • Where are these tools in QGIS?

    Objectives

    • Explain buffer, dissolve, clip, intersect, difference and nearest join, and choose the right one
    • Reproject layers to a CRS in meters and run each operation from the Vector menu and the Processing Toolbox
    • Select features by location and explain how the choice of spatial predicate changes the answer
    • Estimate a population inside a zone with areal weighting in the Field Calculator, and state its assumption
    • Measure straight-line distances to the nearest facility and recognize their limits

    What is geoprocessing?

    Geoprocessing means operations that take one or more spatial layers and produce a new layer: a zone around every store, the parts of tracts inside a city, the distance from each neighborhood to its nearest clinic. A small set of operations covers most everyday GIS work, and every GIS program (QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, GeoPandas, R’s sf) offers the same ones under similar names.

    This episode answers one question with them: how many people in Lafayette and West Lafayette live within 1 mile of a supermarket? The Geoprocessing in Python episode answers the same question with the same data in code, so you can compare results.

    The operations

    Operation Question it answers Output QGIS
    Buffer What is within d meters of each feature? One polygon per feature Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Buffer
    Dissolve What is the combined area, or the total per group? Merged features Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Dissolve
    Select by location Which features touch, contain or lie within another layer? A selection (no new shapes) Vector > Research Tools > Select by Location
    Clip What part of this layer lies inside a boundary? Cut shapes, own attributes only Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Clip
    Intersect Where do two layers overlap? Cut shapes, attributes of both Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Intersection
    Difference What part of A lies outside B? Cut shapes of A Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Difference
    Nearest join What is the closest feature, and how far is it? Each feature plus the nearest match and a distance Processing Toolbox: Join attributes by nearest

    Two habits make the difference between a result you can trust and one you cannot:

    • Clip versus intersect. Both cut shapes. Clip only uses the second layer as a cookie cutter; intersect also copies its attributes onto every piece. Use intersect when you need to know which zone each piece is in.
    • Keep the original area. Once a tract is cut, you can no longer tell what share of it remains. Store its area in a field before any clip or intersect.

    Projection comes first

    A buffer distance and a measured area are in the units of the layer’s coordinate reference system (CRS). Data from the web usually arrives in EPSG:4326, latitude and longitude in degrees. The Buffer dialog says so: next to the distance it shows degrees and a yellow warning sign, and a distance of 1609 would be read as 1,609 degrees. A small value such as 0.015 looks plausible but is still wrong: in Indiana a degree of longitude is about 85 km and a degree of latitude about 111 km, so the “circle” is an ellipse.

    QGIS reprojects layers on the fly so they line up on screen, but the tools work on each layer’s own coordinates. So convert every layer you will analyze to a projected CRS in meters first, with Reproject Layer. For Indiana, EPSG:26916 (UTM zone 16N) is the usual choice for local work. The Foundations QGIS episode and the Data Management module’s Coordinate Reference Systems episode cover the theory.

    Callout

    $area or area($geometry)?

    The Field Calculator offers two ways to measure. $area measures on the ellipsoid set in Project > Properties > General, in the units chosen there. area($geometry) measures in the layer’s own CRS units. In a layer reprojected to EPSG:26916 the two agree closely; in a layer still in degrees area($geometry) returns square degrees. This episode uses area($geometry) so the numbers match the Python version exactly.

    Choosing a distance

    A buffer is only as meaningful as its distance. Common thresholds in access research:

    Distance Roughly Typical use
    400 m (a quarter mile) 5-minute walk Bus stops, small parks
    800 m (a half mile) 10-minute walk Parks, transit stations, corner stores
    1.6 km (1 mile) 20-minute walk Supermarkets in urban areas (the USDA’s urban threshold)
    16 km (10 miles) Short drive Supermarkets in rural areas (the USDA’s rural threshold)

    Choose the distance from the literature or from a policy you are evaluating, write it down, and test whether your conclusion changes with a smaller or larger value. That last step is a sensitivity analysis, and in QGIS it means rerunning one tool with a different number (the Graphical Modeler can chain the steps so you rerun them all at once).

    Selecting by location

    Select by Location selects the features of one layer that pass a spatial predicate against another:

    Predicate (QGIS wording) True when
    intersect The shapes share any point (touching counts)
    are within The feature is completely inside the other shape
    contain The other shape is completely inside the feature
    centroid are within The feature’s center point is inside the other shape (run Centroids first)

    The predicate changes the answer, sometimes dramatically. With the 1-mile supermarket zone in Lafayette, 35 tracts intersect it, only 6 lie completely within it, and 24 have their center inside it. None of these is wrong, but a report that says “24 tracts are near a supermarket” must say which test produced that number.

    From areas to people: areal weighting

    Tracts do not line up with buffers or city limits, so a tract is often split. If 40% of a tract’s area falls in the 1-mile zone, how many of its residents live there? Areal weighting assumes they are spread evenly, so it assigns 40% of the population:

    estimated people in a piece = tract population × (piece area ÷ tract area)

    It is simple and transparent, and it is wrong in a predictable way: people live in houses, not in fields, parks, rivers or parking lots. Areal weighting overestimates people in empty parts of a tract and underestimates them in dense parts. Better methods use smaller units (block groups, blocks) or land cover, a technique called dasymetric mapping; the Raster Analysis episode shows how to summarize land cover by tract, which is the first step.

    Counts, rates and dissolving

    Dissolve merges features. In current QGIS versions the plain Dissolve tool keeps the attributes of one feature and does not add up numbers. To merge and total at the same time, use Aggregate in the Processing Toolbox (or sum in the attribute table, as this episode does). Summing is right for counts (people, households, households without a car) and wrong for rates and medians (poverty rate, median income). For a rate, sum the numerator and the denominator separately and divide.

    Pitfalls

    • Edge effects. The store layer covers only the two cities. A rural tract near the county line may have a supermarket just outside the data, so this episode limits the analysis to the city limits.
    • Straight line is not travel. Rivers, railroads and highways turn a 1-mile straight line into a much longer trip. Grocery Access Part 2 in the Case Studies module measures along roads with QGIS network tools.
    • Centroids are not people. A tract center can fall in a field. Population-weighted centers or smaller units give fairer distances.
    • Temporary layers. Processing results are temporary scratch layers (a small chip icon in the Layers panel) and vanish when QGIS closes. Right-click and choose Make Permanent for anything you want to keep.
    • Data currency. OpenStreetMap stores open and close. Check the data against local knowledge.

    Hands-on: supermarkets within 1 mile

    These steps were checked in QGIS 4.0; in QGIS 3.34 and later the menus are the same. Keep the Processing Toolbox open (Processing > Toolbox): its search box finds any tool by name.

    Part 1: Load the layers from the web

    Use Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer, Source Type: Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc., Type: HTTP/HTTPS/FTP (in QGIS 4 the Type list starts with cloud services, so check it), as in the Foundations QGIS episode, and add these three addresses:

    Layer Web address
    Grocery stores https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/CaseStudies/main/data/grocery_stores.geojson
    City limits https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/CaseStudies/main/data/study_area.geojson
    Tracts with ACS data https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/tippecanoe_tracts_acs.geojson

    The tracts layer already has the 2024 ACS columns joined (total_pop, pop_under18, households, hh_no_vehicle and others); the Foundations episode on tables shows how that join is done. Add an OpenStreetMap basemap underneath if you like.

    Check: 64 store points and one city polygon over Lafayette, 43 tracts covering Tippecanoe County.

    Part 2: Reproject to meters

    1. Open Vector > Data Management Tools > Reproject Layer (or search the Processing Toolbox for it).
    2. Input layer: grocery_stores. Target CRS: click the globe button and choose EPSG:26916 - NAD83 / UTM zone 16N. Leave Reprojected as a temporary layer and click Run.
    3. Rename the result stores_utm (right-click > Rename Layer).
    4. Repeat for the city limits (city_utm) and the tracts (tracts_utm). The dialog remembers the CRS.
    5. Set the project CRS to EPSG:26916 as well (click the CRS button at the bottom right of the window).

    Check: right-click tracts_utm > Properties > Information: the CRS is EPSG:26916 and the units are meters.

    Part 3: Keep only the supermarkets

    1. Processing Toolbox: Extract by attribute.
    2. Input layer: stores_utm; Selection attribute: store_type; Operator: =; Value: Supermarket. Run, and rename the result supermarkets.

    Check: 17 features (open the attribute table, or look at the count after the layer name with Show Feature Count).

    Part 4: Buffer, then dissolve

    1. Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Buffer.

    2. Input layer: supermarkets. Distance: 1609, meters. Segments: 16 (smoother circles; the Python version uses the same). Leave Dissolve result unchecked for now. Run, and name the result buffers.

    3. Open the attribute table of buffers, click the Field Calculator (the abacus icon), and create a new decimal field km2 with the expression area($geometry) / 1000000. Click OK, then the pencil icon to stop editing and save.

    4. Select all rows and look at the Statistics panel (View > Panels > Statistics), choosing the km2 field: the Sum is about 138 km².

    5. Now run Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Dissolve on buffers (no dissolve field). Name it zone and measure it the same way: about 85 km².

    The difference, 53 km², is overlap that would have been counted twice. (The Buffer tool’s own Dissolve result box does both steps at once.)

    Part 5: Select by location

    1. Vector > Research Tools > Select by Location.

    2. Select features from: tracts_utm; where the features: tick intersect; By comparing to the features from: zone. Click Run, then Close.

    3. The status bar and the layer’s attribute table show 35 selected tracts.

    4. Run it again with only are within ticked: 6 tracts.

    5. For the centroid test, run Vector > Geometry Tools > Centroids on tracts_utm (name it centers), then select centers that are within zone: 24 points.

    Clear selections with Edit > Select > Deselect Features from All Layers before moving on.

    Part 6: Store each tract’s original area

    1. Open the attribute table of tracts_utm and the Field Calculator.
    2. New field tract_m2, type Decimal Number (real), expression area($geometry). OK, then stop editing and save.

    This must happen before clipping, because the clipped pieces will copy this field unchanged.

    Part 7: Clip to the city and estimate its population

    1. Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Clip: Input layer tracts_utm, Overlay layer city_utm. Name the result tracts_city.

    2. Check: 39 features. Many are only parts of tracts.

    3. In its Field Calculator, create pop_in_city (Decimal Number (real)) with area($geometry) / "tract_m2" * "total_pop". The Preview under the expression shows the result for the first tract, a quick check that the expression works.

    4. In the Statistics panel, the sum of pop_in_city is about 114,000. The 2020 Census counted about 115,000 people in the two cities, so areal weighting comes close here.

    Part 8: Intersect with the 1-mile zone

    1. Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Intersection: Input layer tracts_city, Overlay layer zone. Name it near_pieces.
    2. Field Calculator: pop_near = area($geometry) / "tract_m2" * "total_pop".
    3. The sum of pop_near is about 77,500, or 68% of the city estimate.

    The pieces also carry the attributes of the zone. Because the zone was dissolved from 17 buffers, those columns (store_name, address and so on) describe just one store and mean nothing here; ignore or delete them. This is the practical difference between Intersection and Clip.

    Part 9: The parts farther than 1 mile

    1. Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Difference: Input layer tracts_city, Overlay layer zone. Name it far_pieces.
    2. In both near_pieces and far_pieces, create nocar_est = area($geometry) / "tract_m2" * "hh_no_vehicle".
    3. Compare the sums: about 4,570 households without a car live within 1 mile of a supermarket and about 1,450 live farther away.
    Callout

    Small differences from the Python version

    Your sums may differ from the Python notebooks in the last digit or two. Buffers are polygons that only approximate circles, and QGIS and GeoPandas place the segment points slightly differently. Differences of a few people are normal; differences of thousands mean a step went wrong (most often a layer still in degrees).

    Part 10: Distance to the nearest supermarket

    1. Select the centers that are within city_utm (Select by Location), then right-click centers > Export > Save Selected Features As (or use Extract by location) to make centers_city: 31 points.

    2. Processing Toolbox: Join attributes by nearest. Input layer centers_city, Input layer 2 supermarkets, Layer 2 fields to copy store_name, Maximum nearest neighbors 1. Run.

    3. Open the result’s attribute table and sort the distance field (in meters, the layer CRS units) from high to low. Census Tract 102.07 is farthest, about 3,820 m from a supermarket; the median is about 1,250 m.

    4. Style the points with Graduated symbology on distance to see the pattern.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Which operation?

    Name the operation (or operations) for each task.

    1. Show the parts of Tippecanoe County that are within 500 m of the Wabash River.
    2. Count the households in each tract that live within 500 m of the river.
    3. Keep only the bus stops that lie inside the West Lafayette city limits.
    4. Find the closest library to each school, and how far away it is.
    1. Buffer the river by 500 m (reprojected first), with Dissolve result ticked if it is made of several segments.
    2. Store each tract’s area, Intersection of the tracts with the buffer, then areal weighting in the Field Calculator on the households field.
    3. Select by Location with are within (or Extract by location to save them as a layer).
    4. Join attributes by nearest, which adds a distance field.
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: A half-mile walk

    Repeat Parts 4 and 5 with a half-mile (805 m) buffer, closer to a 10-minute walk. How many tract centers fall inside the half-mile zone? What does this tell you about walking to a supermarket in Lafayette?

    Buffer supermarkets by 805 m with Dissolve result ticked, then select centers that are within the new zone: 6 tract centers (compared with 24 for 1 mile). Most neighborhoods are not within an easy 10-minute walk of a supermarket, so the result depends strongly on the threshold. This is why the distance should be justified and tested.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Is the estimate too high or too low?

    Census Tract 104 contains most of Purdue’s residence halls and also large areas of lawns and playing fields. Half of the tract’s area lies inside a park’s 800 m buffer, and the buffered half is mostly playing fields. Will areal weighting overestimate or underestimate the residents near the park? What would improve the estimate?

    It will overestimate: areal weighting puts half the residents in the buffered half, but few people live on the playing fields. Better estimates use smaller units (census blocks), or land cover to move people onto developed land (dasymetric mapping, previewed in the Raster Analysis episode). At minimum, report the assumption and check the tract against a basemap.

    Key Points
    • Reproject every layer to a CRS in meters (EPSG:26916 for Indiana) before buffering, measuring or overlaying; on-the-fly display does not change the data
    • Buffer draws zones, Dissolve merges them, Clip and Intersection cut shapes, Difference keeps what lies outside, and Join attributes by nearest finds the closest feature and its distance
    • The predicate in Select by Location (intersect, are within, centroid within) changes the answer; report it
    • Store the original area before cutting, then use area($geometry) / "tract_m2" * count for areal weighting
    • Sum counts, never rates or medians; processing results are temporary until you make them permanent

    Content from Network Analysis

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can a road map be represented as a graph?
    • How do we download and visualize road networks from OpenStreetMap?
    • How do we find the shortest route and measure travel time?
    • How do routes turn into measures of access, and what can go wrong?

    Objectives

    • Explain nodes and edges in a road network
    • Download a drivable network with OSMnx and inspect it as GeoDataFrames
    • Compute shortest paths by distance and by travel time
    • Measure travel time from many locations to one point, the basis of an access study
    • Choose a network type and an access measure that fit the research question, and recognize the assumptions behind them

    Why network analysis?

    Straight line distance is misleading: a store 1 km away across a river may be a 6 km drive. Network analysis measures distance along roads, which is how people actually travel.

    Road networks are stored as graphs:

    • Nodes are intersections and dead ends
    • Edges are road segments, each with a length (and, once added, a speed and travel time)

    Common uses include food and health care access, emergency response times, and transportation planning.

    Thinking in graphs

    A graph is a simple idea: a set of points (nodes) and the connections between them (edges). In a road network, nodes are intersections and dead ends, and each edge is the stretch of road between two of them. Everything else is stored as attributes of the edges:

    Edge attribute Example Used for
    length 212.4 (meters) Shortest path by distance
    highway residential, primary Road type, and a default speed
    maxspeed 30 mph Travel time, where speed limits are mapped
    oneway True Which directions can be traveled
    travel_time 18.3 (seconds) Fastest path, once added

    Three details matter for analysis:

    • Direction. Streets can be one-way, so OSMnx stores roads as a directed graph: a two-way street is two edges, one in each direction. The route from A to B can therefore differ from the route from B to A.
    • Weights. The “shortest” path depends on what each edge costs. With length as the weight you get the shortest route; with travel_time you get the fastest. You can also build your own weights, for example a walking cost that penalizes steep or busy roads.
    • Simplification. OpenStreetMap draws a curving road with many small points. OSMnx removes the points that are not intersections, so each node is a real decision point and each edge keeps its full curved shape and length.

    Choosing the network type

    The network_type argument decides which roads and paths are kept:

    network_type Includes Direction
    "drive" Public roads open to cars One-way rules apply
    "walk" Streets and paths pedestrians can use, including footpaths where they are mapped; no motorways Every edge can be walked both ways
    "bike" Streets and paths where cycling is allowed One-way rules apply

    Pick the network that matches the people you study. A household without a car experiences the walking or transit network, not the driving one, and the two can give very different answers about access.

    Callout

    The same analysis in QGIS

    The Case Studies module’s grocery access case study measures shortest paths and service areas to supermarkets in Lafayette and West Lafayette with QGIS’s network tools, without writing code. Doing both is a good way to see what OSMnx does behind the scenes.

    If you have not used OpenStreetMap tags before, the Data Collection module’s Geocoding episode introduces them.

    1. Download a road network

    PYTHON 

    import osmnx as ox
import networkx as nx

G = ox.graph_from_place("West Lafayette, Indiana, USA", network_type="drive")
print(G.number_of_nodes(), "nodes,", G.number_of_edges(), "edges")
ox.plot_graph(G, node_size=5, edge_color="gray", bgcolor="white")

    network_type can also be "walk" or "bike". The graph is held in memory as G.

    2. Look at nodes and edges as tables

    PYTHON 

    nodes, edges = ox.graph_to_gdfs(G)
edges[["name", "highway", "length"]].head()    # length is in meters

    3. Add speeds and travel times

    PYTHON 

    G = ox.add_edge_speeds(G, fallback=40)   # km/h used where a road type has no speed data
G = ox.add_edge_travel_times(G)          # adds travel_time in seconds to every edge

    4. Find the shortest route between two points

    PYTHON 

    start = ox.nearest_nodes(G, X=-86.9112, Y=40.4247)   # longitude, latitude
end = ox.nearest_nodes(G, X=-86.9290, Y=40.4580)

route = ox.shortest_path(G, start, end, weight="travel_time")
ox.plot_graph_route(G, route, route_color="red", node_size=0)

    5. Measure the route

    PYTHON 

    route_edges = ox.routing.route_to_gdf(G, route)
print(round(route_edges["length"].sum() / 1000, 2), "km")
print(round(route_edges["travel_time"].sum() / 60, 1), "minutes")
    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Shortest or fastest?

    Compute the route between the same two points with weight="length" and with weight="travel_time". Are they the same route? Which is longer in kilometers?

    PYTHON 

    for w in ["length", "travel_time"]:
    e = ox.routing.route_to_gdf(G, ox.shortest_path(G, start, end, weight=w))
    print(w, round(e["length"].sum() / 1000, 2), "km",
          round(e["travel_time"].sum() / 60, 1), "min")

    The fastest route often uses faster main roads and can be a little longer in distance.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Travel time to everywhere

    Use nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(G, start, weight="travel_time") to get the travel time from start to every node. What is the longest drive time (in minutes) within the city?

    PYTHON 

    times = nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(G, start, weight="travel_time")
print(round(max(times.values()) / 60, 1), "minutes")

    From routes to access

    A single route answers “how far is it from here to there?”. Access studies ask a broader question: how easily can people reach the things they need? Network analysis supports several common measures:

    Measure Question Built from
    Nearest facility How far, or how long, is it to the closest store, clinic or school? Paths from each home or neighborhood to every facility, keeping the minimum
    Cumulative opportunities How many jobs or stores can be reached within 15 minutes? Travel times from each origin, counting the destinations under a threshold
    Service area (isochrone) Which streets or areas lie within 10 minutes of a facility? Travel times outward from the facility (Challenge 2 is the start of one)
    Origin-destination matrix What is the travel time between every origin and every destination? Paths for every pair; the basis of the measures above and of gravity models

    Notebook 3c builds a nearest facility measure for grocery stores.

    Getting on and off the network

    Homes, stores and clinics are not nodes. Before routing, each location is snapped to the nearest node with ox.nearest_nodes. This works well in a dense street grid, but check the snapping distance when places are far from a road, such as a store in a large parking lot or a rural farm. The route starts at the snapped node, not at the front door, and a point can snap to a road on the wrong side of a river or highway.

    PYTHON 

    node, dist = ox.nearest_nodes(G, X=-86.9112, Y=40.4247, return_dist=True)
print(node, round(dist), "meters from the network")   # flag large distances

    return_dist reports the distance in the units of the graph. A graph from graph_from_place is in latitude and longitude, where OSMnx measures this distance in meters along the Earth’s surface.

    Assumptions and pitfalls

    A network result is only as good as the network and the assumptions behind it:

    • Speeds are estimates. add_edge_speeds uses mapped speed limits, the average speed of other roads of the same type, or the fallback value. It ignores traffic, traffic lights and turns, so real drive times are usually longer, especially at rush hour.
    • The map may be incomplete. OpenStreetMap is very good in most U.S. cities, but it can miss footpaths, new roads or turn restrictions. Look at the network before trusting it.
    • Edge effects. A network downloaded for one city stops at the city limits. Trips that leave the city and come back, and stores just outside it, are missed. Download a larger area than your study area (for example with ox.graph_from_point and a generous dist, or ox.graph_from_polygon with a buffered boundary), then analyze only the origins inside the study area.
    • Mode and time of day. A driving network says nothing about buses, schedules or sidewalks. Public transit needs timetable data (GTFS) and dedicated tools.
    • Distance is not the whole story. Cost, safety, opening hours and quality of service also shape real access.
    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Which network, which measure?

    A health department asks you to find neighborhoods where older adults without cars live more than 20 minutes from a pharmacy. Which network_type would you use, which access measure, and what would you set or check before trusting the result?

    • The walking network (network_type="walk"), because the people in question do not drive. Ideally you would add public transit as well.
    • A nearest facility measure: the walking time from each neighborhood to the closest pharmacy, flagged where it is above 20 minutes.
    • OSMnx speeds are for cars, so set a walking speed yourself, for example G.edges[u, v, k]["travel_time"] = length / speed, with a speed in meters per second. Older adults often walk more slowly than the 4 to 5 km/h usually assumed.
    • Check that the pharmacy list is complete, download the network beyond the neighborhoods to avoid edge effects, and check the snapping distances of homes and pharmacies.

    Math

    A network is a graph \(G = (V, E)\), where \(V\) is the set of nodes (intersections) and \(E\) the set of edges (road segments). Each edge \(e\) has a weight \(w_e\), such as length or travel time. The shortest path between two nodes is the route whose total weight \(\sum_{e \in \text{route}} w_e\) is smallest. OSMnx finds it with Dijkstra’s algorithm.

    Dijkstra’s algorithm works outward from the start like a ripple. It keeps the best known cost to every node, always settles the unvisited node with the lowest cost next, and then updates the costs of that node’s neighbors. When the destination is settled, its cost is final. This only works when every weight is zero or positive, which is true for lengths and travel times.

    Key Points
    • Road networks are graphs of nodes (intersections) and edges (road segments)
    • ox.graph_from_place downloads OpenStreetMap roads for any named place
    • add_edge_speeds and add_edge_travel_times let you route by time instead of distance
    • nearest_nodes (longitude first), shortest_path and route_to_gdf cover most routing tasks
    • Network distance is more realistic than straight line distance for access studies
    • Match the network type to the people you study, and choose an access measure (nearest facility, cumulative opportunities, service area) that fits the question
    • Check snapping distances and edge effects, and remember that speeds are estimates without traffic

    Notebooks

    Level Notebook What you will do
    Beginner 3a. Road Networks: Nodes and Edges Download, plot, inspect and save a road network
    Intermediate 3b. Shortest Paths and Travel Time Route between two points and map travel time across the city
    Advanced 3c. Travel Time to Grocery Stores Route from every OSM grocery store to the town center

    Content from Spatial Autocorrelation with PySAL

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What does it mean for data to be spatially autocorrelated?
    • How do we tell the computer which places are neighbors?
    • How do Global and Local Moran’s I measure and locate clustering?
    • What choices and pitfalls affect the results?

    Objectives

    • Build Rook, Queen and K-nearest neighbor spatial weights with PySAL
    • Compute and interpret Global Moran’s I and its p-value
    • Read a Moran scatterplot
    • Map statistically significant hotspots and coldspots with Local Moran’s I (LISA)
    • Explain permutation tests, multiple testing and the modifiable areal unit problem

    Why spatial autocorrelation?

    “Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.” (Tobler’s first law of geography)

    Most statistics assume observations are independent. Places are not: a county’s income or median age is usually similar to its neighbors’. Spatial autocorrelation measures how strong that similarity is, and PySAL (the Python Spatial Analysis Library) provides the standard tools.

    Question PySAL method
    Who counts as a neighbor? Spatial weights (libpysal.weights)
    Is there clustering across the whole map? Global Moran’s I (esda.Moran)
    Where are the hotspots and coldspots? Local Moran’s I, LISA (esda.Moran_Local)
    Could the pattern be chance? Permutation tests (p_sim)

    In this episode we use 2023 American Community Survey data for Indiana counties, loaded with a Census API key (see the Census data session for how to get one).

    Why it matters

    Spatial autocorrelation is both a problem and a finding.

    • A problem for standard statistics. Regression and t-tests assume that each observation adds new, independent information. When neighbors are similar, Indiana’s 92 counties carry less independent information than 92 random draws, so standard errors come out too small and results look more significant than they are. Spatial regression models (in PySAL’s spreg package) correct for this.
    • A finding in itself. Clustering says something about the process behind the data: people with similar incomes sort into similar neighborhoods, diseases spread to nearby places, and policies spill across borders. Mapping where clusters are is often the first step of a spatial study.

    Spatial weights: who is a neighbor?

    Before PySAL can compare a place with its neighbors, you must say who the neighbors are. This is the spatial weights matrix \(W\): a table with one row and one column per place, where \(w_{ij}\) is not zero when \(j\) is a neighbor of \(i\).

    Type Neighbors are Good for
    Rook contiguity Polygons that share an edge Regular polygons and grids
    Queen contiguity Polygons that share an edge or a corner Most polygon data, such as counties or tracts (the usual default)
    K-nearest neighbors (KNN) The k closest centers Points, or polygons of very different sizes; every place gets exactly k neighbors
    Distance band Every place within a set distance Points, when “near” has a natural distance

    Two more ideas come up constantly:

    • Row standardization (w.transform = "R") divides each row by the number of neighbors, so each place’s weights sum to 1. A county with eight neighbors and a county with three are then treated alike, and multiplying the weights by the data gives the spatial lag: the average value of each place’s neighbors.
    • Islands are places with no neighbors under a contiguity rule, such as an island county. PySAL warns about them. Drop them, or give them neighbors with a KNN or distance rule.

    1. Build spatial weights

    counties is a GeoDataFrame of Indiana counties with a median_age column, projected to meters.

    PYTHON 

    from libpysal.weights import Rook, Queen, KNN

w_rook = Rook.from_dataframe(counties, use_index=True)    # shared edge
w_queen = Queen.from_dataframe(counties, use_index=True)  # shared edge or corner
w_knn = KNN.from_dataframe(counties, k=4)                 # 4 closest centers

print(w_rook.mean_neighbors, w_queen.mean_neighbors)
w_queen.transform = "R"    # row standardize: each county's weights sum to 1

    2. Global Moran’s I

    PYTHON 

    from esda.moran import Moran

mi = Moran(counties["median_age"], w_queen, permutations=999)
print(f"I = {mi.I:.3f}, p = {mi.p_sim:.3f}")
    • I clearly above 0 with p below 0.05: similar values cluster together
    • I near 0: no spatial pattern
    • I below 0: neighbors tend to be different

    PYTHON 

    from splot.esda import moran_scatterplot
moran_scatterplot(mi, aspect_equal=True)

    Reading the Moran scatterplot

    The scatterplot puts each county’s value on the x axis and its spatial lag (the average of its neighbors) on the y axis, both standardized so that 0 is the mean.

    • The slope of the fitted line equals Moran’s I (with row standardized weights).
    • The four quadrants are the categories that LISA uses below: top right High-High (a high value among high neighbors), bottom left Low-Low, top left Low-High (a low value among high neighbors) and bottom right High-Low.
    • Points far from the line are places that do not fit the overall pattern, and are worth a closer look.

    You can compute the spatial lag yourself:

    PYTHON 

    from libpysal.weights import lag_spatial
counties["lag_median_age"] = lag_spatial(w_queen, counties["median_age"])   # neighbors' average

    Could it be chance? Permutation tests

    PySAL tests significance by permutation. It shuffles the values randomly among the places, for example 999 times, recomputes I for each shuffled map, and counts how often a shuffled map is at least as extreme as the real one. The pseudo p-value is

    \[ p = \frac{M + 1}{R + 1} \]

    where \(M\) is the number of shuffled maps at least as extreme as the observed one and \(R\) is the number of permutations. With 999 permutations the smallest possible p-value is 0.001. Because the shuffles are random, p-values can change slightly from run to run; Moran_Local accepts a seed so that results are repeatable.

    3. Local Moran’s I (LISA)

    PYTHON 

    from esda.moran import Moran_Local
from splot.esda import lisa_cluster

lisa = Moran_Local(counties["median_age"], w_queen, permutations=999, seed=42)
lisa_cluster(lisa, counties, p=0.05)     # only significant counties are colored

    Labels: High-High (hotspot), Low-Low (coldspot), High-Low and Low-High (outliers), and Not significant.

    Local results need care

    Local Moran’s I runs one test per place: 92 tests for Indiana counties, and hundreds or thousands for tracts. With a cutoff of p < 0.05, about 1 place in 20 would look significant even on a completely random map. To be careful:

    • use a stricter cutoff, such as p=0.01;
    • apply a False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction, which lowers the cutoff according to the number of tests;
    • treat significant clusters as places to investigate, not as proof.

    Getis-Ord Gi* (esda.G_Local) is another common hotspot statistic. It finds clusters of high or low values but does not separate outliers the way LISA does.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Rook or Queen?

    Print the Rook and Queen neighbors of the same county, for example w_rook.neighbors[0] and w_queen.neighbors[0]. Why can Queen never have fewer neighbors than Rook?

    Queen counts every county that shares an edge (like Rook) plus any that only touch at a corner. So it always includes all Rook neighbors, and sometimes a few more.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: A second variable

    Compute Global Moran’s I for pct_asian. Is it clustered? Then make its LISA map.

    PYTHON 

    mi2 = Moran(counties["pct_asian"], w_queen, permutations=999)
print(mi2.I, mi2.p_sim)
lisa_cluster(Moran_Local(counties["pct_asian"], w_queen, seed=42), counties, p=0.05)

    A positive I with p below 0.05 means clustering. High-High counties usually sit around large cities and universities.

    Pitfalls

    • The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP). Results change with the units. The same people aggregated to counties, tracts or ZIP codes can show different clusters, or none. State the units you used and, if you can, check another.
    • Small numbers. Rates and estimates for places with small populations swing widely by chance and can create false hotspots. American Community Survey estimates for small areas also have large margins of error. Look at population sizes and margins of error before interpreting a cluster.
    • Edge effects. Places on the edge of the study area, such as border counties, have fewer neighbors, so their local statistics rest on less information.
    • The weights are a choice. Rook, Queen and KNN can give different answers. Try more than one; robust patterns survive the change.
    • Clustering is not causation. A High-High cluster of median age says where older populations are, not why.
    Challenge

    Challenge 3: An outlier tract

    A LISA map of median household income for Marion County tracts shows one tract labeled High-Low. What does that label mean, and what could explain it? What would you check before writing about it?

    High-Low means the tract’s income is well above the mean while its neighbors’ average is below the mean, and the difference is unlikely to be chance under the permutation test. It could be a new upscale development, a gentrifying area, or an affluent enclave next to lower-income neighborhoods. It could also be a statistical artifact: check the tract’s population and the estimate’s margin of error, because a small tract with a large margin of error can produce an extreme value by chance. With hundreds of tracts, also remember that about 1 in 20 can be significant at p < 0.05 by chance alone.

    Math

    Global Moran’s I is

    \[ I = \frac{N}{W} \cdot \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \]

    where \(N\) is the number of places, \(w_{ij}\) is the weight between places \(i\) and \(j\) (non zero only for neighbors), \(W\) is the sum of all weights, and \(x\) is the variable. The top of the fraction is large when neighbors are on the same side of the mean.

    Key Points
    • Spatial weights define who is a neighbor: Rook (edges), Queen (edges and corners), KNN (closest)
    • Global Moran’s I gives one number for clustering across the whole map
    • The permutation p-value tells you whether the pattern could be chance
    • Local Moran’s I (LISA) locates hotspots, coldspots and outliers; always filter by p-value
    • Many local tests produce false positives; use stricter cutoffs or FDR, and treat clusters as leads
    • Results depend on the units (MAUP), the weights, small populations and edges of the study area

    Notebooks

    Level Notebook What you will do
    Beginner 4a. What Is a Neighbor? Spatial Weights Load Indiana counties and compare Rook, Queen and KNN neighbors
    Intermediate 4b. Global Moran’s I Test whether median age is clustered and read the Moran scatterplot
    Advanced 4c. Local Moran’s I and Hotspots Map significant clusters for counties, then for Marion County tracts

    Content from Spatial Clustering

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is spatial clustering and when is it useful?
    • Why must coordinates be in meters before clustering?
    • How do K-Means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN and HDBSCAN differ?
    • When is a cluster of points really a hotspot?

    Objectives

    • Prepare point data for clustering by reprojecting to a meter based CRS
    • Find dense hotspots with DBSCAN and HDBSCAN and recognize noise points
    • Divide points into zones with K-Means and choose k with the elbow method
    • Choose a clustering method that fits the research question
    • Explain how each method works, what it assumes, and how to choose its parameters
    • Recognize the population at risk, data collection effects and other pitfalls in hotspot maps

    Why spatial clustering?

    Clustering finds groups of points that sit close together: crime hotspots, disease outbreaks, clusters of archaeological finds, or concentrations of businesses. It turns thousands of points into a few areas you can describe and compare.

    Method You choose Noise points? Best for
    K-Means Number of clusters (k) No, every point is assigned Dividing an area into zones
    Hierarchical Number of clusters or a cut height No Seeing structure at several scales (small datasets)
    DBSCAN Search radius (eps) and min_samples Yes Hotspots of any shape at a known distance
    HDBSCAN min_cluster_size Yes Hotspots with varying density

    The notebooks use about 200,000 crime reports from the Chicago Data Portal and focus on robbery.

    Points, patterns and the population at risk

    Clustering looks for places where events (robberies, disease cases, archaeological finds) are concentrated. It is related to, but different from, the previous episode: spatial autocorrelation asks whether values attached to areas (such as median age by county) are similar among neighbors.

    Before calling a cluster a “hotspot”, ask what you are comparing it with. Events happen where people are: a busy downtown has more robberies than a quiet suburb partly because far more people pass through it. A dense cluster of points may reflect the population at risk rather than an unusually high risk. Common ways to handle this are to compare with a background (rates per resident or per visitor, or a control set of points such as all reported crimes), or to aggregate the points to areas and analyze rates with the methods from the PySAL episode.

    How the data were collected shapes them too. Crime reports reflect reporting and policing as well as crime itself, and the Chicago portal shows locations at the block level only to protect victims’ privacy, so many reports share exactly the same coordinates.

    1. Load points and reproject to meters

    PYTHON 

    import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np

# read the CSV straight from GitHub into memory (nothing to download)
crimes = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/DataAnalysis/main/data/CrimesChicago20220225.csv")
crimes.columns = crimes.columns.str.strip()
robbery = crimes[crimes["PRIMARY DESCRIPTION"] == "ROBBERY"].dropna(subset=["LATITUDE", "LONGITUDE"])

robbery = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    robbery,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(robbery["LONGITUDE"], robbery["LATITUDE"]),
    crs="EPSG:4326",
).to_crs(epsg=32616)          # UTM zone 16N: x and y in meters

coords = np.column_stack([robbery.geometry.x, robbery.geometry.y])

    Latitude and longitude are angles. One degree of longitude in Chicago is about 85 km while one degree of latitude is about 111 km, so distances in degrees are distorted. Always reproject first.

    2. DBSCAN: density based hotspots

    PYTHON 

    from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

db = DBSCAN(eps=1000, min_samples=50).fit(coords)   # eps in meters
robbery["dbscan"] = db.labels_                       # -1 means noise

    A point with at least min_samples neighbors within eps meters is a core point; nearby core points form a cluster. Choose eps with a k-distance plot (see notebook 5b).

    3. HDBSCAN: no radius needed

    PYTHON 

    from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN

robbery["hdbscan"] = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=50, min_samples=10).fit_predict(coords)

    4. K-Means: zones

    PYTHON 

    from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

robbery["kmeans"] = KMeans(n_clusters=6, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit_predict(coords)

    5. Hierarchical clustering and the dendrogram

    PYTHON 

    from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster

sample = robbery.sample(2000, random_state=1)        # hierarchical is slow on large data
tree = linkage(np.column_stack([sample.geometry.x, sample.geometry.y]), method="ward")
dendrogram(tree, truncate_mode="lastp", p=20, no_labels=True)
sample["hier"] = fcluster(tree, t=6, criterion="maxclust")

    Plot any result with robbery.plot(column="dbscan", categorical=True, markersize=1).

    How the methods work

    DBSCAN

    DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) sorts every point into one of three kinds:

    • a core point has at least min_samples points (counting itself) within eps;
    • a border point lies within eps of a core point but does not have enough neighbors of its own;
    • a noise point is neither, and gets the label -1.

    Core points that are within eps of each other join the same cluster, so clusters can take any shape, following a river or a commercial street.

    Choosing eps. Make a k-distance plot: for every point, find the distance to its k-th nearest neighbor (with k equal to min_samples), sort those distances and plot them. Most points sit on a flat part of the curve; where the curve bends sharply upward (the “knee”), points start to be isolated. The distance at the knee is a good first choice for eps.

    PYTHON 

    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

k = 50                                                    # same as min_samples
dist, _ = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(coords).kneighbors(coords)
plt.plot(np.sort(dist[:, -1]))
plt.ylabel(f"distance to neighbor {k} (m)")
plt.xlabel("points, sorted")
plt.show()

    Choosing min_samples. Larger values ask for denser clusters and label more points as noise. With thousands of points, values in the tens are common; with a few hundred, try 5 to 10.

    DBSCAN’s weakness is that one eps applies to the whole map, so it cannot find both a tight downtown cluster and a looser suburban one at the same time.

    HDBSCAN

    HDBSCAN (Hierarchical DBSCAN) avoids choosing eps. In effect it tries every value of eps at once, builds a tree of how clusters split apart as the distance shrinks, and keeps the clusters that last over a wide range of distances (the most stable ones). You set min_cluster_size, the smallest group worth calling a cluster. It finds clusters of different densities, labels noise as -1, and reports how strongly each point belongs to its cluster (probabilities_).

    K-Means

    K-Means places k centers, assigns every point to its nearest center, moves each center to the mean of its points, and repeats until nothing changes. It assumes clusters that are roughly round and of similar size, and it assigns every point, so outliers pull the centers toward them. The result depends on where the centers start; n_init=10 runs ten starts and keeps the best one.

    To choose k, plot the inertia (the total squared distance from points to their centers) for k = 2, 3, 4 and so on, and look for the elbow where adding clusters stops helping much. The silhouette score (sklearn.metrics.silhouette_score, from -1 to 1) measures how well each point fits its own cluster compared with the next nearest one; higher is better. On large datasets, compute it on a sample with sample_size=2000.

    Hierarchical clustering

    Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters. The linkage rule defines “closest”: single linkage (the nearest pair of points, which tends to make long chains), complete linkage (the farthest pair), average linkage, or Ward (the merge that adds the least variance, which makes compact clusters). In the dendrogram, the height of each join is the distance at which two groups merge; cutting the tree at a height gives the clusters. Memory use grows with the square of the number of points, which is why the example uses a sample.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: K-Means or DBSCAN?

    Map the K-Means and DBSCAN results side by side. Which one would you use to report “robbery hotspots” to a city council, and why?

    DBSCAN (or HDBSCAN). K-Means assigns every robbery to a zone, even isolated ones, so its “clusters” cover the whole city. DBSCAN keeps only dense areas and labels scattered points as noise, which is what a hotspot means.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Adjusting DBSCAN

    Run DBSCAN with eps=500 and eps=1500 (meters). How do the number of clusters and the share of noise points change?

    PYTHON 

    for eps in [500, 1500]:
    labels = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=50).fit(coords).labels_
    print(eps, labels.max() + 1, "clusters", f"{(labels == -1).mean():.0%} noise")

    A smaller eps gives more, smaller clusters and more noise. A larger eps merges clusters into a few large ones.

    Pitfalls

    • Degrees instead of meters. Always reproject first (Section 1).
    • Duplicate locations. Block-level coordinates put many reports on the same spot. Every duplicate counts as a neighbor, which can make an area look denser than it is.
    • Parameters shape the result. Report eps, min_samples, min_cluster_size or k, and check how the map changes with other values (Challenge 2).
    • No significance test. Unlike LISA, these methods do not test whether a cluster could arise by chance. Comparing with random points, or using a scan statistic, is needed for that.
    • Edges. Points near the edge of the study area, such as the city limits or the Lake Michigan shore, have fewer neighbors.
    • Consequences. Hotspot maps can stigmatize neighborhoods and influence where police patrol, which in turn produces more reports in the same places.
    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Reading a k-distance plot

    Your k-distance plot (k = 50) stays fairly flat up to about 800 m and then rises steeply. Which eps would you try first? What would happen with eps=200 or eps=3000?

    Start with an eps of about 800 m, at the knee of the curve. With eps=200, few points have 50 neighbors that close, so most points become noise and only the very densest spots remain as small clusters. With eps=3000, almost every point is a core point, so clusters merge into one or a few very large ones that cover much of the city and say little about hotspots.

    Discussion

    Hotspot or crowd?

    DBSCAN finds a large robbery cluster in the Loop, Chicago’s downtown. Is the Loop a dangerous place, or just a crowded one? What extra data would help you decide?

    Math

    DBSCAN looks at the neighborhood of each point \(p\): all points within distance \(\varepsilon\) (eps). If that neighborhood holds at least min_samples points, \(p\) is a core point. Core points within \(\varepsilon\) of each other join the same cluster, along with the border points near them. Every other point is noise.

    K-Means instead chooses \(k\) centers \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k\) that minimize the total squared distance \(\sum_i \lVert x_i - \mu_{c(i)} \rVert^2\), where \(c(i)\) is the center closest to point \(x_i\). This total is the inertia used in the elbow plot.

    Key Points
    • Reproject to meters before clustering so distances are real
    • DBSCAN and HDBSCAN find dense hotspots of any shape and label scattered points as noise
    • K-Means splits all points into k round zones; choose k with the elbow method
    • Hierarchical clustering shows how groups merge, but is slow on large datasets
    • Pick the method that matches your question: hotspots or zones
    • Choose eps with a k-distance plot and k with the elbow method or silhouette score
    • A dense cluster may reflect the population at risk, duplicate locations or reporting, not high risk

    Intermediate 5b. DBSCAN and HDBSCAN Choose eps, find robbery hotspots and compare with HDBSCAN

    Content from NDVI Analysis

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is NDVI and why is it useful?
    • How do we read Landsat bands and compute NDVI in Python?
    • How can we classify NDVI into land cover groups?
    • What affects NDVI values, and how should they be interpreted?

    Objectives

    • Explain why vegetation is bright in near infrared and dark in red
    • Read raster bands with rasterio and convert them to surface reflectance
    • Compute, map and save NDVI as a GeoTIFF
    • Classify NDVI with thresholds and summarize area by class
    • Describe spectral signatures, image processing levels and resolution
    • Recognize the limits of NDVI (season, clouds, saturation, mixed pixels) when comparing places and dates

    Why NDVI?

    Healthy leaves absorb red light for photosynthesis and strongly reflect near infrared (NIR) light. The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) uses that contrast to measure greenness from satellite images. It is easy to compute, works with most sensors (Landsat, Sentinel-2, MODIS), and is used for crop monitoring, drought, urban green space and land cover change.

    NDVI Typical surface
    below 0 Water, snow, clouds
    0 to 0.2 Bare soil, buildings, roads
    0.2 to 0.4 Sparse vegetation, grass, early crops
    above 0.4 Dense, healthy vegetation

    The notebooks use one Landsat scene over Indiana (Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance). For Landsat 8 and 9, Band 4 is red and Band 5 is NIR.

    How satellites see vegetation

    A satellite sensor measures how much sunlight each patch of ground reflects in several bands, narrow ranges of wavelength. The share of light reflected is the reflectance, from 0 (all absorbed) to 1 (all reflected). Each kind of surface has a typical pattern of reflectance across wavelengths, its spectral signature.

    • Healthy vegetation absorbs most red and blue light, because chlorophyll uses it for photosynthesis, and reflects a little more green, which is why leaves look green. In the near infrared, just beyond what our eyes can see, the internal structure of leaves scatters light strongly, so reflectance jumps to 0.3 to 0.5.
    • Bare soil and pavement reflect a moderate amount, rising gently with wavelength, so red and NIR are similar.
    • Water absorbs nearly all NIR light, so it is dark in that band.

    NDVI uses the steep rise between red and NIR (the red edge) that only vegetation shows.

    Why a normalized difference?

    The plain difference, NIR minus red, already separates vegetation from other surfaces, but it also changes with the brightness of the scene: the sun angle, slopes facing toward or away from the sun, and thin haze. Dividing by NIR plus red cancels much of that brightness effect and keeps every value between -1 and +1, so NDVI from different places and dates is easier to compare.

    From pixels to reflectance

    Landsat images are distributed at different processing levels:

    Product What the values are Use
    Level-1 Digital numbers (DN): calibrated sensor counts, still affected by the atmosphere Needs conversion before indices are compared
    Level-2 surface reflectance Reflectance corrected for the atmosphere, stored as integers Ready for NDVI after applying the scale and offset

    Collection 2 Level-2 values are stored as integers to save space; multiplying by 0.0000275 and adding -0.2 turns them back into reflectance. The value 0 marks pixels outside the scene. Level-2 products also include a QA_PIXEL band that flags clouds, cloud shadows, snow and water. Masking the flagged pixels before analysis stops a cloud from being counted as bare ground.

    Resolution describes how much detail an image holds:

    Landsat 8 and 9 Sentinel-2
    Pixel size (red and NIR) 30 m 10 m
    Red and NIR bands Bands 4 and 5 Bands 4 and 8
    Revisit 16 days per satellite, 8 days with both About 5 days with both satellites
    Archive Landsat images since 1972 (this sensor design since 2013) Since 2015

    1. Read the bands and convert to reflectance

    PYTHON 

    import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import rasterio

# rasterio reads the bands straight from GitHub into memory; nothing is downloaded
LANDSAT = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/DataAnalysis/main/data/landsat"

with rasterio.open(f"{LANDSAT}/band4.TIF") as src:     # red
    red = src.read(1).astype("float32")
    profile = src.profile
with rasterio.open(f"{LANDSAT}/band5.TIF") as src:     # near infrared
    nir = src.read(1).astype("float32")

red[red == 0] = np.nan          # 0 = outside the scene
nir[nir == 0] = np.nan

# Level-2 values are stored as integers; this converts them to reflectance (0 to 1)
red = np.clip(red * 0.0000275 - 0.2, 0, 1)
nir = np.clip(nir * 0.0000275 - 0.2, 0, 1)

    2. Compute and map NDVI

    PYTHON 

    ndvi = (nir - red) / (nir + red)

plt.imshow(ndvi, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-0.2, vmax=0.8)
plt.colorbar(label="NDVI")
plt.title("NDVI, Landsat scene over Indiana")
plt.show()

    3. Save NDVI as a GeoTIFF (optional)

    PYTHON 

    profile.update(dtype="float32", count=1, nodata=np.nan)
with rasterio.open("ndvi.tif", "w", **profile) as dst:
    dst.write(ndvi.astype("float32"), 1)

    Everything above stays in memory. Save a file only if you want to open the result in QGIS; it keeps the scene’s location, so it lines up exactly.

    4. Classify NDVI

    np.digitize gives each pixel a class number. Three break values make four classes, so we need four colors.

    PYTHON 

    from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

classes = np.digitize(ndvi, [0, 0.2, 0.4]).astype("float32")   # 0, 1, 2, 3
classes[np.isnan(ndvi)] = np.nan

colors = ["#2b83ba", "#d7a26b", "#a6d96a", "#1a9641"]   # water, bare, sparse, dense
plt.imshow(classes[::4, ::4], cmap=ListedColormap(colors), vmin=0, vmax=3,
           interpolation="nearest")    # every 4th pixel keeps the plot fast
plt.title("NDVI classes")
plt.show()
    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Five classes

    Classify NDVI into five classes with breaks [0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3]. How many colors do you need?

    Four breaks make five classes, so you need five colors and vmax=4.

    PYTHON 

    classes = np.digitize(ndvi, [0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3]).astype("float32")
classes[np.isnan(ndvi)] = np.nan
colors = ["#2b83ba", "#d7a26b", "#fdae61", "#a6d96a", "#1a9641"]
plt.imshow(classes[::4, ::4], cmap=ListedColormap(colors), vmin=0, vmax=4,
           interpolation="nearest")
plt.show()
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Mask water

    Replace NDVI values below 0 with np.nan and map the result. What is the mean NDVI of land only?

    PYTHON 

    ndvi_land = np.where(ndvi < 0, np.nan, ndvi)
plt.imshow(ndvi_land[::4, ::4], cmap="YlGn", vmin=0, vmax=0.8)
plt.show()
print(np.nanmean(ndvi_land))

    Masked pixels are left blank on the map and ignored by np.nanmean.

    Interpreting NDVI carefully

    • Thresholds depend on place and season. The table at the top is a rule of thumb. A dry grassland in August and a corn field in July can differ widely. Check thresholds against a true color image or a field visit.
    • Saturation. In dense forest and crops, NDVI levels off around 0.8 to 0.9 and stops responding to further increases in leaf area.
    • Soil background. Where vegetation is sparse, the soil underneath strongly affects NDVI. The Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI) and the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) were designed to reduce soil and atmospheric effects.
    • Mixed pixels. A 30 m pixel in a city can contain a tree, a roof and a road. Its NDVI is a blend, so small green spaces such as street trees and yards are underestimated.
    • Clouds and shadows lower NDVI and can be mistaken for bare ground or water.

    Comparing dates: change detection

    Subtracting NDVI from two dates (for example ndvi_2024 - ndvi_2014) maps where vegetation was gained or lost. Use scenes from the same time of year, because crops and trees change through the seasons (their phenology), and use the same processing level, ideally from the same or a cross-calibrated sensor. Small differences of a few hundredths are within the noise; look for large, coherent changes.

    From thresholds to classification

    Thresholding NDVI (Section 4) is the simplest way to classify land cover. Notebook 6c goes further:

    • Unsupervised classification (K-Means) groups pixels with similar values across several bands; you name the groups afterwards.
    • Supervised classification (Random Forest) learns from training samples you label, such as polygons of known forest, water and buildings, and then predicts every pixel. It needs good training data and an accuracy assessment: compare the predictions with reference points that were not used for training, and summarize the agreement in a confusion matrix.
    Challenge

    Challenge 3: NDVI by hand

    Compute NDVI for three pixels and say what each one probably is:

    1. red = 0.08, NIR = 0.40
    2. red = 0.20, NIR = 0.24
    3. red = 0.06, NIR = 0.03
    1. (0.40 - 0.08) / (0.40 + 0.08) = 0.32 / 0.48 = 0.67: dense, healthy vegetation
    2. (0.24 - 0.20) / (0.24 + 0.20) = 0.04 / 0.44 = 0.09: bare soil, a road or a roof
    3. (0.03 - 0.06) / (0.03 + 0.06) = -0.03 / 0.09 = -0.33: water
    Callout

    NDVI changes with the seasons, clouds and the atmosphere. Compare scenes from the same time of year, and use surface reflectance (Level-2) products rather than raw Level-1 values when possible.

    Math

    \[ NDVI = \frac{NIR - Red}{NIR + Red} \]

    NDVI ranges from -1 to +1. Healthy vegetation has high NIR and low red reflectance, which pushes NDVI toward +1. Water reflects more red than NIR, so its NDVI is negative.

    Key Points
    • NDVI compares NIR and red reflectance; for Landsat 8 and 9 these are bands 5 and 4
    • Convert Level-2 values to reflectance (value * 0.0000275 - 0.2) before computing NDVI
    • rasterio reads and writes rasters; reuse the input profile when saving
    • np.digitize turns NDVI into classes; n breaks give n + 1 classes
    • Vegetation’s spectral signature (low red, high NIR) is what NDVI measures; normalizing reduces brightness effects
    • Interpret NDVI with care: thresholds vary, dense canopies saturate, pixels mix, and clouds and seasons change the values
